svg.text: EchoVault — Browser→Server End-to-End Channel · Layered Architecture (v5)
System topology · TLS termination · observer visibility · trust boundary · HPKE seal (RFC 9180) inside TLS 1.3 · prevents a TLS-terminating proxy from reading prompt/reply plaintext
THE STACK (in the browser · top → bottom)
Renders prompt/echo; E2E ON/OFF toggle for the demo.
Framing, monotonic seq, replay-reject, tamper-fail, ratchet.
Seal/Open via hpke-js ⇄ pyhpke; AAD binds context.
Pin server key; sign+verify the transcript (Ed25519).
Outer wss tunnel; protects transport+metadata; ends at proxy.
recipient key skB_x25519 = Bob’s PRIVATE key · GET /pubkey
frames carry { enc, ct } — sealed payload
Sees TLS plaintext ONLY because it
terminates TLS with a CA the browser trusts.
Trust boundary = the process holding the recipient X25519 PRIVATE key (skB_x25519 prompts, skA_x25519 replies) — the echo server still DECRYPTS here.

TLS alone moves that boundary to the proxy; the inner HPKE seal moves it back to the real reader. Network observers & TLS-terminating proxies see ONLY ciphertext when E2E is ON (L1 + L4 = the thesis).

v5: handshake is Ed25519-authenticated against a PINNED key (pkB_ed25519); assumes Alice obtained it via a trusted initial path. Per-message ephemeral keys reduce exposure — stronger forward secrecy / ratcheting is a limitation / stretch (see “Still not protected”).
“E2E” in this demo = browser app → the INTENDED echo-server process. The server still DECRYPTS & reads the prompt (it is the trusted endpoint).
HPKE IN ONE LINE · WHAT’S STILL NOT PROTECTED
HPKE — the one rule you need here
Browser SEALS with the server’s PUBLIC key.
Server OPENS with its own PRIVATE key.
(a public key locks · only the matching private key unlocks)
→ Full key breakdown: see the Alice⇄Bob HPKE flow diagram.
⚠ STILL NOT PROTECTED (limits / out of scope)
Malicious / compromised echo server — it decrypts & reads the prompt
Plaintext SERVER-SIDE LOGS written after decryption
Compromised or served browser JS (code-delivery channel)
Metadata: message timing, sizes, IPs / ports, traffic patterns
Denial of service — proxy can still drop, delay or block traffic
